subtype: Approach: trial and error [Pitfall]
passage:
"Jeevan, shoes on! The van's coming!"
"I can't find my left one, Ma!"
Jeevan opened the cupboard. Shirts, a ball, his raincoat. No shoe. He shut it.
"Did you look under the bed?" called Lalremsiami, his big sister, from the bathroom.
"Wait." He opened the cupboard again. Shirts. Ball. Raincoat. Shut.
"Maybe it's in the cupboard." Open. Shut. Open once more. His chin began to wobble.
Honk! The van was at the gate.
Lalremsiami came out, dripping, looked under the bed and held up the shoe. "Four times in the same cupboard, Jeevan!"
He ran to the van in one shoe, carrying the other.

qa.q: Where did Lalremsiami look to find the shoe?
qa.a: She looked under the bed.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when his chin began to wobble?
qa.a: He felt anxious and frustrated, because the van was coming and the cupboard kept showing the same things.

qa.q: What else could Jeevan try instead of opening the same cupboard again?
qa.a: He could remember which places he has already checked and try a new one, like under the bed, as Lalremsiami suggested.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami see Jeevan's search?
qa.a: She is amazed he looked in the same cupboard four times, and simply checks a new place and finds it.

grounding: Shows a child opening the same cupboard four times in hope, with no track of where he has looked, until someone checks elsewhere.

subtype: Approach: trial and error [Pitfall]
passage: Note to self, Thursday. After yoga, Gautam couldn't find his left shoe. He went to his cubby, looked, came back, then went again. By the fourth look he was near tears and saying, "It must be there." Nothing new was in it any time. I asked, "Which places have you checked?" He only said, "The cubby." Mehak, who was waiting to go out, said she had seen a shoe near the yoga mats. It was there. Tomorrow I'll show the class how to tick off places on their fingers, so nobody looks in one spot again and again.

qa.q: Where did Mehak say she had seen a shoe?
qa.a: Near the yoga mats.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling by his fourth look?
qa.a: He was near tears, so he felt upset and stuck, still hoping the shoe would turn up in the cubby.

qa.q: What does the note-writer plan to change, and why could it help?
qa.a: The note-writer will teach the class to tick off places on their fingers, so children remember where they've already looked and move on.

qa.q: How might Mehak experience the search?
qa.a: Mehak was waiting to go out, so Mehak may have been a little impatient, and glad that remembering the yoga mats ended it.

grounding: Illustrates a child checking the same cubby four times without tracking where he has looked, so the search goes round in circles.

subtype: Approach: copying a peer [Revision]
passage:
Monday. Kamal ran round the flat looking for his sports shoe: kitchen, bathroom, even the fridge. He went to school in sandals.
Wednesday. The shoe was gone again. Lakshmi, his friend from downstairs, waiting at the door, said, "Check the last place you played." Kamal stopped. "Balcony. I played cars there." He ran, and there it was, behind the flowerpot.
Saturday. Kamal couldn't find his cap. He didn't run round the flat this time. He whispered, "Last place I played," went to the balcony, and picked it up off the railing.

qa.q: Where was the shoe on Wednesday?
qa.a: Behind the flowerpot on the balcony.

qa.q: Why did Kamal stop when Lakshmi gave the hint?
qa.a: He felt surprised and hopeful, because the hint made him remember playing cars on the balcony 🙂

qa.q: What else could Kamal do so things don't go missing so often?
qa.a: He could bring his shoes back to the door after playing; the hint helped him search with a reason instead of at random.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi see the quick find on Wednesday?
qa.a: Lakshmi was waiting at the door, so the quick find probably felt satisfying, knowing the hint saved them time.

grounding: Shows a child using a friend's hint to check the last place he played, which turns a random search into a reasoned one he then repeats.

subtype: Approach: copying a peer [Revision]
passage: The lights went out just as Ujjwal needed his shoe for football class. He flashed the torch everywhere: under the bed, in the bathroom, inside the washing machine. Nothing. His friend Sumit was waiting downstairs, shouting up through the dark. "Hurry!" "I can't find my shoe!" Sumit called, "Check the last place you played!" Ujjwal stood still with the torch. "Balcony. I was kicking the ball against the wall." He shone the beam on the balcony floor. The shoe lay beside the ball. Next time, he told himself, last place first.

qa.q: Where did Ujjwal shine the torch before Sumit's hint?
qa.a: Under the bed, in the bathroom and inside the washing machine.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling while he flashed the torch everywhere?
qa.a: He felt rushed and panicky, with the lights out and Sumit shouting to hurry.

qa.q: What would you change first in how Ujjwal searched?
qa.a: Start with the last place he played, as he tells himself at the end, instead of shining the torch everywhere at random.

qa.q: What was it like for Sumit, waiting downstairs?
qa.a: Sumit was impatient in the dark, and his shouted hint turned out to be what ended the wait.

grounding: Illustrates a friend's hint to check the last place played changing a child's random search into a reasoned one.

subtype: Approach: retracing the steps of the day [Thinking]
passage:
Dear Diary, 14 August
Big panic today. At lunch my blue water bottle was gone. Afreen said, "Just take mine, Sangeeta," but Amma will ask where it is. So I sat on the stairs and thought backwards. Lunch: no bottle. Maths class: I don't remember drinking. PT: yes! Sir made us girls run three rounds, and I drank half the bottle on the bench by the ground. After that I ran to the line when the bell rang. So I went back down during the break. There it was on the bench, warm from the sun. Afreen and I shared it on the way up. Thinking backwards works!

qa.q: Where did Sangeeta find the bottle?
qa.a: On the bench by the ground, warm from the sun.

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta sit on the stairs instead of taking Afreen's bottle?
qa.a: Sangeeta was worried that Amma would ask about the lost bottle, so she wanted to find it and calmly thought backwards through the day.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do so the bottle isn't left behind after PT again?
qa.a: Pick it up before joining the line, or check the bench whenever the bell rings; thinking back found it, but a habit would stop it happening.

qa.q: How might Afreen see the search?
qa.a: Afreen offered a quick fix with a spare bottle, but ended up sharing the found one, so Afreen likely felt glad it worked out.

grounding: Shows a girl thinking back through her day to where she last drank and finding her water bottle on the bench by the PT ground.

subtype: Approach: retracing the steps of the day [Thinking]
passage: Halfway home along the canal road, Neelam's shoulder felt light. Her steel water bottle, the one Nani had bought at the mela, was gone. Deepak, her cousin, groaned. "Now we'll be late." Neelam stopped under the neem tree and shut her eyes. Where did I drink last? Not in class; Masterji doesn't allow it. At lunch I drank from the hand pump. Then PT, on the ground behind the school. I was so thirsty after the race, I sat on the bench and drank. After that, the bell. "The bench," she said. They walked back. The bottle was there, next to a sleeping dog.

qa.q: Where did Neelam drink at lunch?
qa.a: She drank from the hand pump.

qa.q: What might Neelam have been feeling when her shoulder felt light?
qa.a: She was probably worried and upset, since it was the steel bottle Nani had bought at the mela.

qa.q: What else could Neelam try if thinking back hadn't worked?
qa.a: She could ask the teacher or classmates the next day; thinking back worked because it narrowed the search to the bench after the race.

qa.q: How does Deepak see the problem?
qa.a: Deepak groans that they'll be late, so to him the lost bottle is mostly an annoying delay.

grounding: Illustrates a girl retracing her day in her head, remembering drinking after PT, and finding her bottle on the bench.

subtype: Approach: searching the same place again and again [Pitfall]
passage: Last Tuesday, in the middle of a drawing test, my eraser disappeared. I was sure it was in my bag. I opened it and dug through the books. Not there. I zipped it, waited, and opened it again, as if it would appear. I did that five times. My little sister Ankita, in the class below, passed the door and hissed, "Bhaiya, check your pocket!" I shook my head; I knew it was in the bag. "Yusuf, five minutes left," Ma'am said, and by then I had smudged my lines with my thumb. At home I found the eraser. It had been in my pencil case the whole time.

qa.q: Where had the eraser been the whole time?
qa.a: It had been in the pencil case the whole time.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf keep opening the bag after it wasn't there?
qa.a: Yusuf felt so sure the eraser had to be in the bag that he got stuck, growing more flustered as the test ran out.

qa.q: What would have worked better than checking the bag again?
qa.a: Checking a new place each time, like the pencil case or a pocket as Ankita suggested; the same bag gave the same answer five times.

qa.q: How might Ankita see her brother brushing off the tip?
qa.a: Ankita offered a quick idea and was waved away, so she may have felt ignored, and later partly proved right that he needed to look elsewhere.

grounding: Shows a boy searching his school bag five times, sure the eraser is there, while never checking his pencil case, and losing time in a test.

subtype: Approach: searching the same place again and again [Pitfall]
passage: Tuition note, Saturday. During the map worksheet, Jomon put up his hand: his eraser was missing. He unzipped his bag, searched, zipped it. Then again. By the fifth time he was pulling books out and slapping them down, saying, "It's in here, I know it." Sumit offered his own, but Jomon refused. Ten minutes went by and his map had only two rivers. When I asked him to stand and shake out his shirt, the eraser dropped from his pocket. He went red. Next week I'll teach the group to check a new place each time, not the same one.

qa.q: How many rivers were on Jomon's map after ten minutes?
qa.a: His map had only two rivers.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when the eraser dropped from his pocket?
qa.a: He went red, so he probably felt embarrassed after insisting so firmly it was in the bag.

qa.q: What else could Jomon have tried after the first bag search?
qa.a: Checking his pocket or pencil case, or borrowing Sumit's eraser and looking later; searching the same bag cost him ten minutes.

qa.q: How might Sumit see Jomon refusing the eraser?
qa.a: Sumit was trying to help, so Sumit may have felt brushed off and puzzled.

grounding: Illustrates a boy searching his bag five times, certain of the eraser, while it sits in his pocket, costing him time and patience.

subtype: Approach: searching one place at a time in order [Action]
passage: Hiroshi's recorder was missing, and music class started right after lunch. His heart thudded, but he took out a scrap of paper and wrote: 1. bag, 2. desk, 3. bus, 4. lost and found. Leila watched. "Why a list?" "So I don't run around." He emptied his bag: no. He checked inside his desk, even the back corner: no. At the bus bay, he asked the driver, who was eating a rice ball and shook his head. Last came the lost-property box outside the school office in Osaka. Under a pile of gloves lay a blue recorder with his name taped on. Hiroshi let out a long breath.

qa.q: What four places did Hiroshi write on his list?
qa.a: His bag, his desk, the bus and the lost and found.

qa.q: What does Hiroshi's long breath at the end suggest he felt?
qa.a: He felt relieved after the tension of the search, glad the list had led him to the recorder 🙂

qa.q: What else could Hiroshi try if the lost and found had been empty?
qa.a: He could ask the music teacher or classmates; the list would still help, because it shows which places are already ruled out.

qa.q: How does Leila see Hiroshi's list?
qa.a: Leila is curious and asks why he needs it, so the list may look odd at first, but it shows a calm way to search.

grounding: Shows a child checking one place at a time, bag, desk, bus, then lost and found, so he searches without panicking.

subtype: Approach: searching one place at a time in order [Action]
passage: At the hostel, Varun's ID card vanished the night before exams, and he couldn't enter the hall without it. Ujjwal, his roommate, said, "Just tell the warden it's gone." Varun's hands were shaking, but he tore a page from his rough book and wrote: bag, study-hall desk, school bus, lost and found. He tipped out his bag on the bed: pens, a comb, no card. In the study hall he checked his desk, then the one beside it. At the bus bay, the conductor let him look under the seats. Nothing. Last of all, the lost-property tray at the warden's office. His card was right on top, its strap snapped.

qa.q: Where was Varun's card in the end?
qa.a: In the lost-property tray at the warden's office, right on top, with its strap snapped.

qa.q: What do Varun's shaking hands suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He felt anxious and scared about missing the exam, but he steadied himself by writing a list.

qa.q: What else might Varun do before the next exam?
qa.a: He could fix the strap and keep the card in one pocket of his bag; the list worked because it stopped him running in circles.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal see Varun's search?
qa.a: Ujjwal suggested just telling the warden, so Ujjwal may be surprised the list found the card without any fuss.

grounding: Illustrates a boy searching one place at a time in a set order, bag, desk, bus, lost and found, instead of wandering in a panic.

subtype: Approach: asking friends and teachers if they have seen it [Action]
passage: Class 6B diary, Monday. Parul came to me before the first bell: her geometry box had been missing since Friday. She had already asked Hrithik, her deskmate, who hadn't seen it. I suggested a note. She wrote in big letters, 'LOST: blue geometry box, P. Sharma sticker on lid,' and stuck it by the door. By lunch, a Class 8 student stopped by to say she'd seen one near the library. Parul went with her and came back holding it up. I told Parul that asking early and asking widely was the right call. She has promised to write her name inside the lid too.

qa.q: What did Parul's note say?
qa.a: LOST: blue geometry box, P. Sharma sticker on lid.

qa.q: What might Parul have been feeling when she came back holding the box up?
qa.a: She seemed relieved and pleased that asking around and the note had worked 😊

qa.q: What else could Parul try if nobody had seen it?
qa.a: She could check the school lost and found or retrace where she went on Friday; asking widely worked because many people were looking out.

qa.q: How does the note-writer see Parul's approach?
qa.a: The note-writer thinks asking early and widely was the right call, and adds the idea of a name inside the lid.

grounding: Shows a girl asking her deskmate and the class teacher and putting up a note, which leads someone to tell her the box is near the library.

subtype: Approach: asking friends and teachers if they have seen it [Action]
passage:
Wednesday night
My geometry box was gone after the maths period. Compass, protractor, everything! I asked Lakshmi, my deskmate, first. She shook her head and helped me look under the benches. Then I asked Mrs D'Souza. She said, "Jyoti beti, write a note and put it by the door." So I did: LOST, green geometry box, stars on the lid. Just before home time, a boy from 7A knocked and said he saw one on the reading table near the library. I ran. It was there, next to a pile of atlases! Tomorrow I'm writing my name inside the lid.

qa.q: Where did the boy from 7A see the box?
qa.a: On the reading table near the library.

qa.q: How can you tell Jyoti was upset when the box went missing?
qa.a: Writing 'Compass, protractor, everything!' shows Jyoti felt panicky and worried about losing all the tools at once.

qa.q: Which step made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: The note by the door, because it reached people outside the class, like the boy from 7A who had seen the box near the library.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have felt helping Jyoti look?
qa.a: Lakshmi hadn't seen it but still searched under the benches, so she probably felt concerned and keen to help.

grounding: Illustrates a girl asking her deskmate and teacher and posting a note, which brings word that her box is near the library.

subtype: Approach: panicking and blaming others [Pitfall]
passage: Nazia, come sit. You think your Nana Raghav never did anything silly? When I was nine, in Lucknow, we had a spelling test and my new green pencil was gone. I didn't look. I just turned to my bench partner, Babu, and said loudly, 'You took it! Give it back!' The whole class turned. Babu's ears went red. He emptied his pockets right there: two marbles and a string. Masterji made us sit down. Then I lifted my notebook to start, and there was the pencil, lying under it all along. I couldn't look at Babu for the whole test. I said sorry at lunch, but it took days before he sat close again.

qa.q: What did Babu find when he emptied his pockets?
qa.a: Two marbles and a string.

qa.q: What was young Raghav feeling when he found the pencil under his notebook?
qa.a: He felt ashamed; he couldn't look at Babu for the whole test after accusing him in front of everyone.

qa.q: What could young Raghav have done before accusing Babu?
qa.a: He could have taken a breath and checked his own desk and notebook first; one quick look would have found the pencil and spared Babu.

qa.q: What was it like for Babu to be accused?
qa.a: Babu was humiliated in front of the class, his ears went red, and he stayed hurt for days, keeping his distance afterwards.

grounding: Shows a boy quickly accusing his bench partner of taking his pencil, then finding it under his own notebook and feeling ashamed.

subtype: Approach: panicking and blaming others [Pitfall]
passage: The practice test had a timer on the board, twenty minutes, and Lalit's pencil was gone. His stomach flipped. Shankar, his friend at the next desk, was writing fast with a blue pencil. "That's mine," Lalit hissed. "Give it." Shankar stared. "It's my own!" The invigilator looked up. "Silence, both of you." Shankar's cheeks burned and he bent over his paper. Lalit pulled his notebook closer to start with a borrowed pen, and his own pencil rolled out from underneath. Green, not blue. Lalit's face went hot. He wrote the rest of the test without looking sideways, rehearsing a sorry in his head.

qa.q: How long was the practice test?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling when his pencil rolled out from under the notebook?
qa.a: His face went hot, so he felt ashamed and guilty for accusing Shankar without proof.

qa.q: What should Lalit do next, and why?
qa.a: Say sorry to Shankar properly after the test and admit the pencil was under his notebook; the quick blame hurt a friend and wasted the start of the test.

qa.q: How was the accusation for Shankar?
qa.a: Shankar was blamed and told off for something he didn't do, so his burning cheeks suggest he felt embarrassed and wronged.

grounding: Illustrates a boy panicking over a missing pencil and accusing his friend, then finding it under his own notebook and feeling ashamed.

subtype: Approach: staying calm and thinking where he usually puts it [Thinking]
passage: Farhan, you lose your keys every week, so listen to your old Dadu Jagdish. When I was eleven, I was the one who let my little sister in after school. One day I stood at our door in Nagpur, and the key wasn't in my pocket. Chhoti started to cry. My heart was pounding, but I took one long breath and asked myself: where do I always keep it? On the hook inside the window. I reached through the bars: empty. Next, the shoe rack by the door, where I sat each morning. I lifted my old canvas shoe, and the key clinked out of the toe. Chhoti stopped crying mid-sob.

qa.q: Where did young Jagdish find the key?
qa.a: It clinked out of the toe of the old canvas shoe on the shoe rack.

qa.q: Why did young Jagdish take one long breath?
qa.a: His heart was pounding and Chhoti was crying, so he felt panicky, and the breath helped him calm down enough to think.

qa.q: Which choice in the story made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Stopping to ask where he always kept the key; it gave him two sensible places to check instead of a frantic search.

qa.q: What was the lost key like for Chhoti?
qa.a: Chhoti was stuck outside and scared enough to cry, and stopped mid-sob the moment the key appeared.

grounding: Shows a boy calming himself with a breath, thinking where he normally keeps the house key, and finding it inside his shoe on the rack.

subtype: Approach: staying calm and thinking where he usually puts it [Thinking]
passage: Rain was pouring off the stairwell roof, Akash was soaked, and the flat door wouldn't open without the key. His phone had died at lunch. Parveen Aunty from next door peered out. "Lost it, beta?" Akash wanted to kick the door. Instead he pressed his back to the wall and breathed in slowly. "Where do I always put it?" he said aloud. "The hook in my bag. Or the shoe rack, if I came home and went out again." The bag hook was empty. He bent to the rack by the door and tipped up his football boots. The key dropped out of the left one. Akash laughed out loud.

qa.q: Why couldn't Akash call anyone?
qa.a: His phone had died at lunch.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when he wanted to kick the door?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and stressed, soaked by the rain and locked out.

qa.q: What else could Akash do to avoid getting locked out?
qa.a: Keep the key in one fixed place, like the bag hook, every time; staying calm and thinking of his usual spots found it quickly.

qa.q: How might Parveen Aunty see the way Akash handled it?
qa.a: Parveen Aunty came out expecting trouble, and would probably be impressed that he calmed down and found it himself.

grounding: Illustrates a boy breathing slowly, thinking aloud about where he normally puts his key, and finding it inside his boot on the rack.

subtype: Approach: deciding a place for each item to avoid losing [Revision]
passage: Gargi, your Ammamma Leela was once the worst pencil-loser in Madurai. In one week I lost three: one at the bus stop, one in the temple mandapam, one under a bench at school. Each time, I had just put it down somewhere for a moment. My appa, who bought them from his small salary, sighed and said nothing, and that was worse than a scolding. So on Sunday I sat and thought: when did they get lost? Always when I set them down anywhere I liked. From then on my pencil tin lived in the front pocket of my cloth bag, and each pencil went back the moment I finished. I didn't lose another that term.

qa.q: Where did Leela lose the three pencils?
qa.a: One at the bus stop, one in the temple mandapam and one under a bench at school.

qa.q: How did young Leela feel when her appa sighed and said nothing?
qa.a: She felt guilty, and it was worse than a scolding, because he bought the pencils from his small salary.

qa.q: What choice in the story turned things around, and why did it work?
qa.a: Deciding the pencil tin always lived in the front pocket, because it stopped her setting pencils down wherever she liked.

qa.q: How might Leela's appa have seen the change that term?
qa.a: After sighing over three lost pencils in a week, her appa would notice no more were lost, and would likely feel relieved and proud.

grounding: Shows a girl who, after losing three pencils in a week, sees that casual setting down causes the losses and gives her pencils one fixed place.

subtype: Approach: deciding a place for each item to avoid losing [Revision]
passage: By Thursday Preeti had lost three pencils, and the stationery shop was shut for Eid until Monday. Exams started on Saturday. Her friend Rafiq from the next building held out his last one. "This is the only one. Don't lose it." Preeti turned it over and thought. Where had the others gone? One left on the canteen counter, one on the bus seat, one dropped by the water cooler. Every time, I just put it down wherever. That night she emptied the front pocket of her school bag, slid the pencil case in, and told herself: it lives here, always. On Saturday the pencil went back into the case after every paper.

qa.q: Why couldn't Preeti buy a new pencil?
qa.a: The stationery shop was shut for Eid until Monday.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when Rafiq handed over his last pencil?
qa.a: She probably felt anxious and a little guilty, knowing it was the only one and that exams started on Saturday.

qa.q: What else could Preeti do to keep the pencil safe during exams?
qa.a: Check her case before leaving each room; the fixed place worked because she had spotted that the losses came from putting pencils down anywhere.

qa.q: How does Rafiq see lending his last pencil?
qa.a: Rafiq trusts her, but is worried enough to warn 'Don't lose it', so the loan matters to him.

grounding: Illustrates a girl noticing that her lost pencils were all put down casually, and deciding her pencil case always stays in the front pocket.

subtype: Approach: reporting to the school lost and found [Action]

Thursday. Ramesh bhaiya found Kunal in the corridor, holding up a grey sweater. "Blue stripe. KUNAL M." Kunal pulled it on right there.

subtype: Approach: reporting to the school lost and found [Action]
passage: Gurpreet, you ask why I stitch your name into every jersey? Listen to your Dadaji Jeevan. When I was ten, in Amritsar, I lost the maroon sweater my mother had knitted all winter. I was afraid to tell her. A classmate said, 'Go to the office, there's a box.' So I went, knees shaking, and told the clerk: maroon, cable pattern, and my name, J-E-E-V-A-N, stitched in white thread inside the neck. The peon, old Harnam, lifted out a heap of caps and mufflers, then held up my sweater. 'This one has a name. Easy,' he said. I ran home wearing it.

qa.q: What did the lost sweater look like?
qa.a: It was maroon, with a cable pattern and the name stitched in white thread inside the neck.

qa.q: Why were young Jeevan's knees shaking at the office?
qa.a: He was afraid, both of losing the sweater his mother had knitted all winter and of having to tell her.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped most, and why?
qa.a: Going to the office and describing the sweater and the stitched name, because it let the peon pick it out of a heap straight away.

qa.q: How did Harnam see the sweater with the name?
qa.a: For Harnam a name made the job simple; he said 'This one has a name. Easy' and handed it back.

grounding: Illustrates a boy going to the school office's lost and found, describing his sweater and the name inside, and the peon returning it.
